| Close the incomplete request | Report resolved | Lead remains open | Honest terminal state |

### Field 06 expansion — interaction with other plan packages

The profile-to-plan table should include the exact plan register entry for every distinct system. Do not rely on a broad thematic match. Search integrated, partially integrated, and active plan indexes for the same location, cast, objective, initializer, route, save field, and UI surface. If an existing plan owns the result, send the profile card to that owner as a candidate content contribution.

The start framework depends on a working campaign bootstrap and save-slot contract. It may also depend on difficulty, current objective graph support, map knowledge, communications, medicine, power, outpost, or food state. Verify each against live code and data at package creation. An integrated plan does not guarantee that a public API exists for scenario initialization.

### Field 07 expansion — profile compare, confirm, and fail behavior

The comparison screen has a small stable set of columns: premise, first decision, supported systems, time pressure, optional objectives, and save behavior. A profile with a missing dependency is disabled with the name of that dependency. A profile with a content-only limitation can remain available if its opening path still works and the limitation is plainly stated.

Confirmation summarizes only the changes the start contract will make. On failure, keep the prior campaign and provide a safe retry or back path. After a successful start, show the selected profile and first objective before advancing time. Reopening the browser cannot regenerate the seed or reapply owner initializers.

### Field 08 expansion — tutorial copy and fair challenge labels

Use short tutorial keys that are specific to the first action: review a source; inspect the owner status; compare two supported choices; confirm the commitment; review the returned result. The player can close each prompt. Reopening guidance uses the current help path and does not duplicate progress state.

Challenge labels name conditions, not rank: “uncertain starting report,” “limited route window,” “shared access,” or “stock on hold.” Provide the exact meaning next to the label. A harder condition never removes an action without explaining the source. If the first task can fail, make the recovery or terminal state discoverable.

### Field 09 expansion — objective and save test matrix

Cover graphs with one branch, multiple optional branches, expired optional task, unresolved primary fact, rejected owner initialization, and a missing catalog row. Cover saves before initialization, after successful start, during an objective, after an owner receipt but before display refresh, and after callback. Compare resume with new start so they cannot silently share identity.

Measure graph traversal and validation with 1, 6, 12, and 24 profiles and 8, 20, and 40 objective nodes each. The largest diagnostic includes long history and localized text. The browser should not poll objective owners continuously while idle.

### Field 10 expansion — content director and integrator checklists

The content director checks distinct premise, specific source, reachable first action, clear branch, side-task purpose, character knowledge, prose tone, and callback. The integrator checks owner API, save identity, rollback, determinism, route, UI lifecycle, plan claims, and focused verification. Either reviewer can keep a profile disabled without discarding its authored material.

The anthology target is six playable openings, six primary objective graphs, 36 distinct optional task cards, six closeout scenes, and a bounded callback set. These counts are targets for gradual authoring and are accepted only when each row adds a different action or owner result. A profile with no unique gameplay relationship is merged into another profile or delivered through the current campaign.

## Pass 8 — Scenario data readiness and campaign review tools

### Field 01 expansion — profile teaching goals

Each scenario should teach one relationship among systems through play. Coldwater teaches that information quality and allocation are separate: a better measurement can change confidence without automatically changing the supply. Relay teaches that communication availability and message permission are separate. Clinic teaches that a travel plan, an offer of care, and a recipient’s choice are separate. Kilowatt teaches that a reading and a service restriction are not interchangeable. North Watch teaches that presence and recorded duty are related but not identical. Grain teaches that a warning and an item disposition require different authorities.

The scenario must still be enjoyable after the player understands its teaching goal. Do not make every profile a tutorial with a quiz. Once the player has taken a first action, the rest of the arc should let them choose how much evidence to gather and which optional task to pursue.

### Field 02 expansion — scenario data readiness levels

| Level | Meaning | Allowed use |
|---|---|---|
| Concept | Premise only; owners unverified | Planning discussion |
| Content draft | Scene and objective rows drafted | Narrative review |
| Reference checked | IDs exist in current catalogs | Data review |
| Consumer traced | Every action has a runtime route | Integration review |
| Save resolved | Identity and restore behavior known | Package formation |
| Playable slice | End-to-end owner results observable | Focused implementation |
| Release candidate | Accessibility and performance reviewed | Release decision |

No plan author may describe a Concept or Content draft as playable. This vocabulary helps the long-running expansion remain accurate as it grows.

### Field 03 expansion — candidate data keys by profile

| Profile | Opening record | Objective root | Callback key |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coldwater | scenario_coldwater_brief | coldwater_review_reports | coldwater_return_check |
| Relay | scenario_relay_brief | relay_inspect_signal | relay_verified_reply |
| Clinic | scenario_clinic_brief | clinic_review_request | clinic_contact_followup |
| Kilowatt | scenario_kilowatt_brief | kilowatt_review_fault | kilowatt_stability_check |
| North Watch | scenario_watch_brief | watch_compare_records | watch_next_handoff |
| Grain | scenario_grain_brief | grain_trace_warning | grain_disposition_review |

All keys remain proposed and must match naming and schema conventions if promoted. A row can be deferred if the current objective system does not support its condition cleanly.

### Field 04 expansion — closeout scene variants

| Profile | Verified outcome | Disputed outcome | Deferred outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coldwater | A source and rule are confirmed | Two draw accounts conflict | Inspection not available |
| Relay | Sender and allowed reply confirmed | Identity remains partial | Service waits for access |
| Clinic | Visit or handoff accepted | Request source conflicts | Route window expired |
| Kilowatt | Owner reports stable service | Reading remains unreliable | Specialist not available |
| North Watch | Handoff and duty are reconciled | Witness accounts differ | Assignment remains open |
| Grain | Stock disposition accepted | Warning provenance incomplete | Alternate stock unavailable |

Each scene describes what the player learned, which owner result was received, and what remains unresolved. Avoid grading the player or assigning a global success score.

### Field 05 expansion — optional task completion rules

An optional task is complete only when its evidence or action receipt arrives. “Talk to a person” can be a task only if the person provides a source, permission, or meaningful choice. “Visit a location” requires inspection or arrival evidence. A task can be mutually exclusive with another objective, but the conflict should be visible before commitment.

| Task rule | Example | Player feedback |
|---|---|---|
| one-time evidence | Read a dated note | Source attached once |
| repeatable inspection | Recheck after a campaign day | New observation identified |
| mutually exclusive | Publish or withhold message | Conflict disclosed before action |
| expiring window | Arrive before access closes | Expiry and fallback shown |
| optional branch | Verify alternate source | Main goal remains open if skipped |
| canceled action | Player withdraws request | No owner mutation is claimed |

### Field 06 expansion — unblocking and reuse report

Prepare a one-page report for each candidate plan dependency. It identifies the scenario objective, the integrated authority it exercises, any incomplete plan that owns a missing producer or consumer, and the exact acceptance criterion the content might unblock. Mark any dependency that is decision-blocked or currently claimed. The report does not authorize editing another package’s files.

Possible integration value includes making an accepted system reachable earlier, providing a realistic path through save/restore, validating a UI route, adding missing authored rows, or exposing a missing event consumer. A profile that only retells an existing integrated feature has no unblock value.

### Field 07 expansion — starting and ending consistency

The initial objective list appears after successful initialization and reflects the owner receipts actually returned. If an optional initializer was rejected, the objective can offer a valid alternate route or the start fails before activation. The debrief links each outcome to its owner surface and labels any unresolved fact.

Browser and debrief should use the same profile title and content revision. Restart shows the next eligible save slot and start summary. The game must not return to a browser with a partially active campaign if one required initialization stage failed.

### Field 08 expansion — player comprehension and input paths

Review the whole route using keyboard only, controller only, and screen-reader labels where supported. Verify that objective branch relationships have readable names, not only line connectors. A long briefing can be scrolled without losing access to start, back, or close. Validation errors announce their result and return focus to the invalid profile detail.

The comprehension review asks whether a player can name the primary objective, identify one optional task, explain one uncertain starting fact, and predict what the start action changes. If they cannot, revise the profile card before adding more story text.

### Field 09 expansion — data validation and replay envelope

Validate unique profile, event, and objective IDs; all references; finite objective graphs; supported setting IDs; and required owner action names. Check a profile with an optional missing node and a profile with a required missing node. The first may remain available with an explicit omission only if the graph still works; the second is disabled.

Replay tests compare initial canonical state, objective availability, first owner receipts, and save identity across equal seed and settings. Restart and resume must remain separate operations. A profile revision update cannot reorder objectives in a saved run without a migration.

### Field 10 expansion — authoring release dossier

The release dossier has one page per profile with premise, source references, first five actions, optional branches, expected owner results, fallback, save revision, test matrix, accessibility review, and unresolved decisions. A portfolio page shows shared systems and verifies that profile one does not require profile two.

The first release remains one profile plus a focused set of optional objectives. Add another only after the current profile can be started, resumed, canceled before commitment, played to an honest closeout, and compared against the same-seed replay. The anthology grows by proven content packages rather than by making every profile active at once.

## Pass 9 — First-playable profile authoring packet

### Field 01 expansion — first ten minutes

The first ten minutes introduce the profile premise, source of uncertainty, and one available player action. Avoid starting with a long briefing, several unrelated notifications, or multiple locked objectives. The player should be able to inspect the source, reach a current owner view, and understand what will happen if they defer.

### Field 02 expansion — start-state checklist

Before activation, confirm the selected profile, referenced revision, save slot, supported preferences, owner initialization results, first objective, and initial date. A failed required step leaves the campaign inactive. A canceled confirmation leaves every existing campaign untouched.

### Field 03 expansion — opening prompt examples

| Profile | First prompt | First action |
|---|---|---|
| Coldwater | Two readings disagree about when the source was measured | Inspect source records |
| Relay | A signal uses a name the current log does not recognize | Check message provenance |
| Clinic | The request names a visit but no specific action | Ask the contact what is wanted |
| Kilowatt | The gauge and maintenance note differ | Inspect the service |
| North Watch | The outgoing shift record is incomplete | Verify who is present |
| Grain | The label does not show its revision date | Trace the warning |

### Field 04 expansion — opening character knowledge

For each opening speaker, record what they saw, what they heard from someone else, what they do not know, and what they hope the player will do. A contact can be mistaken without being dishonest. Dialog branches should follow evidence and the player’s question, not hidden personality scores.

### Field 05 expansion — objective entry checks

The first objective appears only when its source exists and its action is supported. Optional objectives appear with their expiry conditions, if any. Mutually exclusive options are displayed before commitment. A scenario can begin with an unresolved objective but must provide an explicit safe defer path.

### Field 06 expansion — package dependency card

One dependency card per owner lists the exact start command, accepted inputs, receipt, save behavior, fallback, and current plan status. A missing public initializer is a decision gate. The scenario cannot directly construct another system’s runtime object or copy its mutable state.

### Field 07 expansion — first result summary

After the opening action, show what the current owner confirmed, what the player decided, and which objective changed. If nothing changed, say that the action was informational and provide the next available step. Keep the first result on the campaign surface long enough to understand, then make it available in history.

### Field 08 expansion — fail-soft behavior

If optional content is absent, the primary profile can continue when its graph remains complete. If a required source or owner action is absent, the start is disabled. The player receives a clear explanation and can return to profile comparison without creating a partial save.

### Field 09 expansion — opening sequence review

Review a fresh start, canceled start, invalid profile, save conflict, reload after first result, and new start in a separate slot. Compare equal seeds for identical canonical opening state. Measure profile validation and first-result latency on the current supported hardware profile.

### Field 10 expansion — first-playable handoff

The first-playable packet contains one profile, its first five scenes, root objective and branches, four optional tasks, first callback, source/owner map, save tests, and browser wireframe. It is ready only when a new player can reach a real owner result within the opening sequence and explain what remains unknown.

## Pass 10 — Campaign run support and objective outcome details

### Field 01 expansion — active-run support

The scenario title and primary goal remain visible in the campaign summary after the player leaves the browser. The player can review the starting premise, source uncertainty, and profile revision without restarting the run. This makes a short campaign readable across multiple sessions.

### Field 02 expansion — objective result contract

Each objective result is one of completed, incomplete, canceled, failed, or unresolved, with a source and next action. “Failed” is used only when the player’s action or a real condition closes the path. Missing content is a validation error, not a narrative failure.

### Field 03 expansion — closure rows

| Objective | Valid closure | Unresolved closure |
|---|---|---|
| Verify source | Owner accepts observation | Evidence remains disputed |
| Prepare visit | Team/route accepted | Contact or route unavailable |
| Inspect service | Owner returns result | Inspection not yet scheduled |
| Reconcile record | Current record accepted | Sources remain in conflict |
| Disposition stock | Food/inventory result | Review remains pending |

### Field 04 expansion — continuity between scenes

Each scene reads the objective receipts available at the time it begins. If the player arrives without an expected receipt, use a fallback scene that asks what is known now. Do not repeat the opening as if time had not passed.

### Field 05 expansion — optional task exit

An optional task can be completed, declined, expire, or remain unresolved. Its debrief names which occurred. The primary objective remains available unless the task was an explicit prerequisite shown before commitment.

### Field 06 expansion — active campaign compatibility

New scenario content does not change a campaign started under a different profile. Shared quest IDs and owner effects must be namespaced or otherwise collision-safe under the current catalog rules. Active profiles retain their content revision.

### Field 07 expansion — resume surface

Resume opens the active campaign summary and current objective. Start opens profile selection. These commands remain distinct in label, focus order, and save behavior. A completed profile can be replayed only into a valid separate run.

### Field 08 expansion — accessibility of objective state

The objective summary reads required and optional counts as text. Graph branches include accessible names and state labels. A controller user can move from a result to its next node and back without losing focus.

### Field 09 expansion — revision behavior

Review a profile content update while a run is active, after a run is completed, and before any run starts. Existing runs keep their graph or follow an explicit migration. New starts validate the latest supported revision.

### Field 10 expansion — run archive handoff

At closeout, archive the profile ID, revision, seed reference, terminal result, optional outcomes, and owner receipts through the current save/history owner. Store only what is required to resume or explain the run.

## Pass 11 — Expansion scenario anthology: new premises, playable contracts, and review gates

This pass adds a second anthology layer without duplicating the six starter premises already written in this plan. Coldwater, Relay, Clinic, Kilowatt, North Watch, and Grain remain the initial set. The following six profiles are later candidates with different opening pressures and owner combinations. They are not enabled content, and each must be checked against current integrated plans, partial plans, catalogs, and active claims before production. Their purpose is to expose variety requirements and integration seams, not to assert that each system is missing.

### Field 01 expansion — profile differentiation through player verbs

A scenario profile earns a place in the library when it changes the player’s first three useful verbs, not just the opening paragraph. Two scenarios can share the same location or owner and still be distinct if one asks the player to compare provenance while another asks the player to coordinate a durable handoff. Conversely, changing weather description or character names does not create a new scenario if the player repeats the same query, choice, and result.

The anthology should cover different cognitive shapes: inspect, negotiate, schedule, prepare, preserve, delegate, revisit, and close. Every profile states its core verb, supporting verbs, pressure source, first observable outcome, and what remains uncertain at the end. A profile that cannot define these separately from its premise should be merged into the better-supported scenario or deferred as a branch.

### Field 02 expansion — launch contract with explicit dependency failure

Before launch, validate the profile revision and all required references, query the current campaign slot, check each owner’s preflight contract, and collect initialization receipts. A profile can use optional systems, but an absent optional owner should remove only that optional objective. Required owner refusal prevents launch and returns the slot to its prior state.

Candidate failure messages should identify the broken dependency in player language. “The work roster is not available for this start” is preferable to a raw class or file name. A developer diagnostic may add the precise catalog ID and owner response through existing local diagnostics. Launch must never partly grant items, set a campaign flag, and then return to the browser as though nothing happened.

### Field 03 expansion — six later scenario cards

| Working profile | Opening situation | Distinct first verbs | Main dependency questions |
|---|---|---|---|
| A Shift Left Open | A departing shift has not signed off a shared station; the next crew is waiting | Inspect, contact, hand off | Can a current duty owner represent accepted and rejected handoffs? |
| The Measure Twice Rule | Two crafted components were made from different material records and only one has a traceable source | Compare, inspect, document | Can current crafting/inventory history expose provenance? |
| A Roof for the Reading Room | A small archive collection must move before site access changes | Prioritize, pack, relocate | Can existing storage/site owners confirm capacity and movement? |
| The Long Return Signal | A distant group sent a message that arrives after its original request is no longer current | Reconcile, respond, close | Can radio and chronicle preserve send, receipt, and response times? |
| Work in Public | A repair needs an open work area that competes with a planned gathering | Schedule, negotiate, notify | Can construction/site and event owners expose conflicting use? |
| The Borrowed Cart | A shared cart has been used by several crews, but only one return is recorded | Trace, request, account | Can inventory and journal show custody without a duplicate item ledger? |

These are intentionally different from the first anthology’s water measurement, signal authentication, clinic dispatch, power triage, watch roster, and food inspection. Similarity review still occurs before implementation because the game’s current integrated plan corpus may already cover one of these situations.

### Field 04 expansion — scenario beat sheets with multiple outcomes

**A Shift Left Open.** The opening shows a service station ready for use but no signed handoff. The outgoing worker says the task is finished; the incoming worker says a tool setting changed. The player can inspect the existing task record, ask both workers to state what they observed, or let the incoming shift defer the station. A supported handoff produces a receipt; otherwise the scenario can conclude with the station unavailable and the disagreement preserved. The story rewards a clear boundary, not an assumed culprit.

**The Measure Twice Rule.** A crafted replacement fits the same station, but its material provenance is unclear. The player checks current inventory and crafting records, then decides whether to install, hold, or request another part. If the current owner can expose item provenance, the scenario demonstrates it. If it cannot, launch remains blocked for this profile rather than simulating a source. The human arc follows an apprentice who is embarrassed by the missing note and a mentor who insists that documentation should make repair safer, not shame the worker.

**A Roof for the Reading Room.** Site access will change after a scheduled repair, while a set of records is stored in the affected room. The player inventories the collection only through the current storage owner, confirms an alternate location, and chooses what must be moved first. The scenario does not invent archive capacity. One branch moves the collection before the work; another asks the site owner to delay if supported; a third records an unavailable destination and protects only what the owner permits. A callback explains which voices or dates are now available for future play.

**The Long Return Signal.** A message arrives with a stale request and no direct answer to a later clarification. The player compares timestamps, checks whether the sender is still reachable, and chooses to send a brief acknowledgement, ask a new question, or close the request with a transparent note. A message delivered late is not misreported as a timely rescue. The outcome reveals how a communication delay changed another group’s plan, while leaving the sender’s intent uncertain if no reply arrives.

**Work in Public.** A repair crew and a resident group both reserve a shared space on the same day. The player checks current site/event ownership, asks each group whether it can move, and proposes a schedule only if both owners allow it. The public notice distinguishes confirmed times from a proposal. A no-agreement ending remains playable by relocating or postponing one activity through its owner. The character arc follows a new coordinator learning to announce uncertainty before people travel.

**The Borrowed Cart.** Three crews remember using a cart, but only one has a written return. The player can inspect item state, request a handoff from the last recorded custodian, or declare its location unknown. A later report can resolve the location or remain unknown. No new cart is spawned as a quest reward. The narrative explores the difference between shared ownership and unrecorded responsibility.

### Field 05 expansion — supporting objective sets

Each candidate profile gets three optional objectives, one per information, logistics, or relationship dimension. They are not extra mandatory steps in disguise.

| Profile | Information objective | Logistics objective | Human follow-up |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shift Left Open | Compare the outgoing and incoming task notes | Move an accepted tool only through its owner | Let the next crew choose the confirmation wording |
| Measure Twice | Trace the item’s current catalog identity | Request a supported replacement quote | Ask the apprentice what should be recorded next time |
| Reading Room | List records through the storage owner | Reserve a confirmed destination | Tell the archivist which items could not be moved |
| Return Signal | Compare sent and received timestamps | Queue or send a supported reply | Ask the recipient whether a new request is still wanted |
| Work in Public | Read the two reservation sources | Publish only a confirmed schedule | Record each group’s preferred notice channel |
| Borrowed Cart | Compare custody receipts | Arrange a supported transfer | Ask crews to agree on a future check-in habit |

An objective’s completion path must remain valid when its parent optional system is absent: the profile can hide the objective or replace it with a plain, truthful journal note, depending on the current content contract. Do not patch the profile with fake operational success.

### Field 06 expansion — current-plan collision review protocol

Each new profile receives a four-column collision record: existing plan or feature, current evidence, candidate overlap, and disposition. Disposition values are merge, reuse existing content, defer, verify no overlap, or rejected duplicate. Relevant searches start from scenario titles, premise nouns, verbs, owner classes, catalog IDs, and accepted integration plans. A title search alone is insufficient because an integrated feature may be named differently.

Potential overlap candidates for inspection include work roster and apprenticeship, inventory provenance and crafting, archives and site storage, radio schedules and chronicle, public events and construction schedules, and item custody and shared equipment. These names are research topics, not claims about current code. Mark a premise “cleared” only when the current data, code, and plan index are checked. A stale or archived design document cannot authorize a duplicate subsystem.

### Field 07 expansion — browser filters and detail cards

The browser can offer filters for estimated session length, primary verb, pressure type, owner families, narrative focus, and replay compatibility only if those labels come from validated profile metadata. Filters are descriptive, not difficulty multipliers. Detail cards show: premise; what is known; what is uncertain; first three verbs; likely decision type; whether the scenario introduces a new system; profile revision; required and optional owners; and a non-spoiler note about replay or irreversible choices.

Do not expose unsupported completion percentages. A card for an unavailable profile explains whether it is locked due to progression, content validation, or a missing dependency. The user-facing message must not expose internal file paths. A scenario remains discoverable in the library only if the game can provide a truthful reason why the player cannot start it.

### Field 08 expansion — fair scenario challenge

Each profile defines its information budget: which facts are certain at launch, which are incomplete, how the player can improve confidence, and which facts may remain permanently unknown. A meaningful challenge asks the player to act with this uncertainty in view. It does not hide the prerequisite, shift the goal after commitment, or create an irreversible penalty the browser did not disclose.

Before an irreversible choice, show its direct consequence and any supported alternative. Do not predict outcomes beyond known owner behavior. A missed optional objective can create a story callback but cannot silently make a required owner command unavailable. Profile tests include keyboard-only selection, controller back behavior, text scaling, color-independent status, focus restoration after launch failure, and whether the opening prompts interrupt a critical existing notification.

### Field 09 expansion — anthology-scale memory and replay

Profiles share campaign rules but keep run identity and authored revision clear. The active save remembers which profile and profile revision started it through the current campaign/save owner. Replaying a completed profile follows current save-slot rules and must not overwrite another active run without the established confirmation. A profile update cannot reorder past objective receipts or rewrite journal history.

At anthology scale, load profile metadata separately from long scene text if the current content loader supports that pattern. Build validation should inspect all required references once and reuse results where permitted. Run-time objective evaluation should react to owner events or bounded checkpoints, not scan every graph on every frame. The 6 later candidates extend the original 6 to a target pool of 12, but 12 is a content planning target rather than a production requirement or performance claim.

### Field 10 expansion — anthology decision gate and evidence table

The approval table has one row per profile and records: owner queries checked; plan collisions reviewed; required content records present; optional content behavior; start rollback evidence; primary result; save identity; accessibility review; measured launch/load behavior; and current status. Status is not inferred from prose completeness. Use draft, premise-checked, content-valid, owner-ready, integration-ready, playable, or retired as the review vocabulary only if those terms align with repository workflow.

Promote one new profile at a time. The first should exercise a current end-to-end seam without requesting a new architecture decision. The remaining five wait until the first has passed launch/cancel/resume review. If all six can use the existing campaign and quest contracts, close the framework proposal and deliver content. If any profile needs new campaign identity or a new save section, stop for the signed architecture decision required by the active workflow.


## Pass 12 — Scenario authoring production sheets, branching proof, and library progression

This pass provides a reusable production packet for the later anthology candidates. It does not create a campaign manager, objective runtime, new save format, score, or difficulty rule. The six original profiles and six later candidates remain separate content groups until current-plan collision checks accept their combination.

### Field 01 expansion — objective verbs and result promises

Each profile’s first screen contains a plain-language promise with four parts: situation, first useful verb, likely result type, and uncertainty that will remain. Examples:

- “A shift ended without a clear handoff. Inspect the record and decide whether the station should reopen.”
- “A replacement part has no traceable source. Compare its record before deciding whether to install it.”
- “An archive room will become unavailable. Confirm a destination before deciding what to move.”
- “A late signal carries an old request. Check the dates before sending a reply.”
- “A repair and a gathering need the same space. Verify both schedules before committing.”
- “A shared cart has no complete return note. Trace its last confirmed custody.”

The promise is not flavor text alone. It constrains objective authorship: the first required interaction must use the stated verb; the result card must report the actual owner response; and the unresolved clause must not be “solved” by a hidden narrative flag.

### Field 02 expansion — objective graph review cards

For each node, the author records entry source, owning system, visible prompt, supported command, completion receipt, failure receipt, optional children, and exit condition. A node should have one primary completion predicate. If completion requires three unrelated owners, consider splitting the interaction or documenting an explicit orchestration owner. Do not put those decisions into generic panel callbacks.

A graph review includes reachable paths from start to a primary ending, paths that skip optional content, a missing-dependency path, a declined-action path, and a save/resume boundary. Cycles require a documented exit or revisit condition. Repeated information gathering must produce new evidence or be optional. A scenario may end with an unresolved question if the primary player promise has been truthfully answered.

### Field 03 expansion — profile data production sheet

Every profile manifest proposal includes:

- Stable working ID and human-readable title.
- Revision and status: draft, premise checked, content valid, owner ready, or playable.
- One-sentence premise and player promise.
- Required and optional owner families.
- Required location, character, item, message, and objective references.
- Opening state requests with rollback expectations.
- First primary objective and one visible receipt.
- Optional objective list and omission behavior.
- Closing conditions, including unresolved outcome.
- Save identity and profile-revision behavior.
- Browser summary, content warnings where supported, and accessibility notes.
- Collision-review sources, owner evidence, and last review date.
- Removal and migration behavior for future versions.

This sheet is documentation until the current schema and campaign owner approve a machine-readable form.

### Field 04 expansion — six profiles as branching proof

| Profile | Main branch | Alternative branch | Stable ending | Required evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shift Left Open | Reconcile and accept handoff | Keep station unavailable pending inspection | Incoming crew knows the exact limit | Duty/task receipt |
| Measure Twice Rule | Trace part and install if supported | Hold the part and request a new source | Part status and provenance uncertainty are visible | Inventory/crafting owner response |
| Roof for the Reading Room | Move records to a confirmed site | Delay work if current owner permits | Records are accounted for, or missing destination is explicit | Storage/site receipts |
| Long Return Signal | Send a caveated response | Close the old request and ask for a new one | Late timing remains clear | Radio/chronicle receipts |
| Work in Public | Move one event through accepted schedule | Postpone one commitment with agreement | Both groups know the confirmed schedule | Event/site receipts |
| Borrowed Cart | Confirm the cart’s current custodian | Record location unknown and change handoff practice | No false return is claimed | Inventory transfer or unresolved record |

The authored branch cannot promise an owner result that the branch does not query. If the work-order, event, or custody owner cannot expose a result, the corresponding profile remains disabled.

### Field 05 expansion — three side tasks for every profile

The twelve later profiles will share an authoring pattern but not repeated content. For each of the six later profiles, include:

1. A source-check task that improves provenance or timestamp clarity.
2. A logistics task that uses a current inventory, route, schedule, or storage command.
3. A human callback in which an affected person responds to the player’s choice.

The task must have a distinct entry condition, named owner, completion evidence, optional status, and closure text. An optional task that simply asks the player to perform the same command again is removed. An optional task that changes another owner’s state is only allowed when that owner explicitly accepts the command.

### Field 06 expansion — current plan portfolio and promotion gates

Before adding a profile to the launch set, inspect the live plan index and partial implementation logs for the systems it needs. The record should state: which active plans overlap; which partially integrated plans expose a usable seam; which completed integrations already meet the need; which decision-blocked work is excluded; and who accepts the scenario integration. The result may show that an owner is already ready, that prose should be attached to another plan, or that a profile duplicates existing content.

Do not classify a profile as a plan unblock simply because it exercises a system. An unblock has an exact acceptance criterion, evidence from current source, and an accepted handoff to its owner. If the profile reveals a genuine missing producer or consumer, preserve it as a finding and request a bounded package through current governance.

### Field 07 expansion — browser progression and informed selection

A new player sees three groupings: ready to start, available after current progress, and not ready. The last grouping is optional and appears only when it can state a helpful reason. Profile detail presents the first decision, not a full spoiler. Starting a profile shows a final summary of selected difficulty and supported accessibility settings from existing preferences, current save slot, and any irreversible setup choice. Backing out changes none of these.

A player can resume an active scenario directly. If more than one run can exist under the current save contract, the browser identifies each by profile, last simulation step, and current objective. It does not create a parallel profile history or run slot. A finished scenario can be replayed only with the established confirmation path and an accurate description of what will be replaced or preserved.

### Field 08 expansion — comprehension and accessibility scripts

Conduct a plain-language review by asking a reader to describe the profile’s opening uncertainty, first action, commitment, and result after seeing only the browser card and first in-game panel. If the reader cannot tell a proposed action from a committed one, revise the interface. If a color cue carries unique information, add a shape, label, or pattern. If a keyboard or controller path cannot reach the first action, the profile is not ready even if its graph is valid.

Tutorial copy is tied to action context. It can be revisited from the profile’s current UI but does not appear repeatedly after completion unless the player asks for it. Large text, contrast, reduced motion, and focus behavior are inherited from current preferences. Scenario content may supply alternate phrasing only through the established localization/accessibility contract.

### Field 09 expansion — reproducibility and replay diagnostics

A profile’s opening bundle must be stable across runs given the same seed, save condition, and current owner inputs. Dynamic references are resolved in a documented order. Optional objectives cannot be selected through unordered iteration. A failed start records which stage refused and confirms that no earlier stage left partial state.

A replay comparison records selected profile revision, initial owner receipts, objective graph revision, first action, and terminal outcome. It checks that a content update does not rewrite an active save. Performance review measures browser metadata load separately from start initialization and first scene render. If the run graph grows, measure node evaluation and history serialization before optimizing. Do not precompute and persist derived UI values unless the existing save owner requires it.

### Field 10 expansion — production acceptance checklist

A profile is accepted for production only when:

- Current-plan collision review is dated and has source evidence.
- Required catalog references validate against existing data.
- Launch can cancel or roll back safely through the current owner contract.
- First action uses an actual gameplay command.
- Primary outcome comes from an owner receipt.
- Optional content may be skipped without a dead end.
- Refusal, missing dependency, and unresolved endings are readable.
- Profile identity and revision survive the existing save/load path.
- Browser and gameplay views obey current accessibility and focus behavior.
- One complete run can be replayed without duplicate rewards, messages, or objectives.
- Performance observations are measured on a named build if scale has become material.
- The accepting owner and exact claimed files are recorded.

The anthology remains a proposal if any required owner, validator, or save seam is unknown. A long list of scenarios cannot compensate for a missing launch contract; one truthful profile is the first milestone.


## Pass 13 — Campaign character arcs, branch prose, and authoring acceptance

This pass supplies reusable story production guidance for both the original six profiles and the six later candidates. It does not expand the number of fields or imply that any candidate profile is integrated.

### Field 01 expansion — campaign-level story shape

A profile has a local problem and a wider question. The local problem must be answerable through current gameplay; the wider question can remain open across multiple runs or future authored content. A scenario should not require the player to finish every optional task to understand either. Its character arc follows a change in responsibility, knowledge, or trust behavior, rather than a binary moral alignment.

Each run begins with a person asking for something concrete. The middle reveals a limit or conflicting account. The player chooses what to verify, commit, delay, or decline. The ending names the actual result and leaves a thread for a later callback. The scenario can end without a triumphant resolution, provided the player can describe what their action changed.

### Field 02 expansion — branch conditions and state safety

Every branch predicate maps to a current owner receipt, an explicit profile setup fact, or a player choice retained by the existing campaign owner. Branches based on absent conditions are removed until the owner provides them. A branch can be cosmetic if it changes a character’s response but not gameplay state; label it as such in the authoring sheet.

A scene cannot set its own completion condition before the owner result returns. On load, a completed node stays completed, an in-flight action is reconciled against its owner, and an unresolved action returns a safe prompt. Re-entering a scene cannot award the same reward or resend the same message.

### Field 03 expansion — story packet template

For each scene, record: profile and revision; scene key; speaker; location; entry evidence; prior choice; current owner query; text before action; action label; direct consequence; refusal result; no-contact result; owner failure result; text after result; journal line; optional callback; accessibility notes; and localization length band. This sheet helps writers and implementers agree on what the scene can truthfully say.

The template also marks whether a line is diegetic, UI instruction, system status, or debrief. A character should not speak like a debug panel, and a system status should not hide behind character voice when precision matters.

### Field 04 expansion — branching scene samples

**Shift Left Open, first scene.** The outgoing worker says: “The station is ready. I changed the latch after the last alarm, but I did not see the new crew test it.” The player can ask for the previous receipt, invite the new crew to inspect, or keep the station closed. If the duty owner confirms a handoff, the worker says: “Good. Put the inspection beside my note so nobody has to guess which one came later.” If it refuses, the closeout says the station remains unavailable. The scene never declares it ready based on dialogue alone.

**Measure Twice Rule, midpoint.** The apprentice says: “It fits. I wrote down the alloy name, not where we got this piece.” The mentor replies: “A fit is evidence about shape. It is not a receipt for the source.” The player may query inventory/crafting provenance, hold the part, or request a supported replacement. If provenance is not exposed, the scenario stops at a clear uncertainty and does not simulate an install.

**Roof for the Reading Room, ending.** The archivist says: “The catalog moved with the crates, but the room is still closed.” The player sees the separate storage and site results. If both owners confirm, the ending says the archive is accessible at the new site. If only the crates moved, the ending says the collection is stored but its destination is not open. If the move could not happen, the archivist identifies which records remain and asks for a later plan.

**Long Return Signal, final reply.** The sender says: “I asked about the east gate before the work crew moved. That answer came after the gate changed.” The player can acknowledge the timing, ask whether the question still stands, or close the original request. A delivered message is reported only when the channel owner confirms delivery. The old request remains readable as a time-stamped artifact.

**Work in Public, schedule scene.** The host says: “If we start after the meeting, the crew loses their last hour of light. If we start before it, the room is not ours.” The player sees current schedule ownership and may request a supported move. The host accepts or objects based on the actual result; a panel cannot force both commitments to fit.

**Borrowed Cart, callback.** A crew member says: “I remember leaving it at the north store. I do not have a receipt.” If the current inventory confirms that location, the character signs the new handoff. If not, the journal records the statement as testimony and leaves location unknown. The story avoids presenting memory as canonical inventory.

### Field 05 expansion — optional quest callbacks across profiles

Optional tasks can seed future dialogue when a real receipt exists. Comparing source dates may let an archivist ask for the player’s notation style. Returning a tool may lead a crew to use the same current custody process. Sharing a notice with consent may prompt a resident to request a correction. Declining a meeting move may lead the host to prepare a second location for another day. These callbacks must remain low-coupling: a missing optional receipt removes one line, not a required ending.

A callback matrix lists the source receipt, scene that consumes it, fallback line, and whether the callback is local to a run or persistent across campaigns. Cross-campaign memory requires an existing owner and explicit design approval. Do not create a meta-progression flag simply to remember a line.

### Field 06 expansion — authoring and integration collaboration

The writer delivers source text, state variants, and exact intended meaning. The system owner identifies available facts and refuses unsupported state. The integrator maps conditions to current IDs and validates data references. The UI owner checks focus, status, and layout. One reviewer checks the full player path from scenario browser through the closing scene. The handoff records where a line was simplified because an owner exposes less detail than the fiction first requested.

### Field 07 expansion — profile browser narrative

The browser card is a compact contract, while the opening scene carries character voice. Profile tags cannot promise that every optional system is present. A “return visit” label means the scenario includes an authored later scene; it does not promise a route if the travel owner can refuse it. A content note summarizes difficult themes and optionality without revealing the outcome.

After a failed start, the player returns to the same selected profile, settings, and slot if still valid. A developer diagnostic may show failed references. The player-facing error describes the unmet condition without exposing implementation names.

### Field 08 expansion — review script for a cold reader

Give a reviewer only the browser card and opening sequence. Ask: What do you know? What is uncertain? What can you do first? What action would be irreversible? What does the result mean? Which optional task can be skipped? If their answer exceeds what the game knows, remove misleading wording. If they cannot identify the player’s first action, revise the card or the opening UI before adding more prose.

Accessibility review asks the same questions with keyboard/controller navigation and non-color labels. Captions and written source details carry essential information where supported. The first decision remains reachable without audio.

### Field 09 expansion — saved narrative and content versioning

Store stable scene IDs and current owner receipts through the existing campaign history. Avoid saving display text as the authoritative state; a corrected translation should not rewrite the result. If a content revision changes a required branch, the current migration owner must define whether the active run keeps the old graph, migrates safely, or becomes unavailable for new progression. No active run may silently jump to a different ending because a scene key was renamed.

### Field 10 expansion — final authoring pass gate

Before a profile enters production, one reviewer checks premise uniqueness against integrated and partial plans; one reads the branching scripts; one checks that every condition exists; and the integrator traces the player command to the owner receipt and save path. The scenario is ready only when the browser promise, in-game decision, debrief, and persistent record describe the same event. The content pack may contain many polished scenes while still being blocked from launch; the status report must keep content-complete separate from playable.


## Pass 14 — Worked scenario launch, campaign run, and save trace

This worked run illustrates the scenario browser and one profile from selection through ending. It is an acceptance example, not evidence that the launch path or profile exists.

### Field 01 expansion — browser to first action

The player opens the library and sees the original six candidate starts and the six later candidates only if each has passed its content and owner gates. The profile “A Shift Left Open” is marked draft until collision review is complete. Its browser card states: “A shared station has no accepted shift handoff. Inspect the record and decide whether the station should reopen.” It lists one required duty/task owner and optional journal context. It does not show a play button when a required owner is unavailable.

The player opens details. The panel distinguishes known facts—a departing worker left a note and a new shift is waiting—from uncertainty—the station was not observed after the latch changed. The first action is “Review the handoff record.” It is an information action and does not commit to opening the station. The player backs out. The library returns to the same card and slot selection; no campaign state changes.

### Field 02 expansion — validation and initialization

The player reopens the profile and selects an available save slot. The launch flow validates profile revision, required task reference, site reference, objective graph, and current owner readiness. The campaign owner returns a preflight receipt. If any required reference fails, the flow returns to the browser with an explanation and no partial setup. A diagnostic identifies the failed ID through existing local tooling.

On a valid start, the owner accepts the initial handoff facts and returns a campaign identity. The browser transitions to the opening scene only after all required receipts arrive. A save made immediately after initialization contains the profile and revision through the current save owner. It does not contain a duplicate copy of site, duty, inventory, or relationship state.

### Field 03 expansion — opening choice and objective chain

The departing worker’s note says the latch was changed after a previous alarm. The incoming crew says they have not tested it. The player can inspect the current record, request a new owner-supported check, or keep the station unavailable. The first objective completes when the owner returns a valid handoff fact, not when the dialogue has been read.

If the record is incomplete, the player can ask the outgoing worker to clarify, if the current communication/quest path supports it. If not, the scenario proceeds with that uncertainty. The objective graph exposes a primary route to a safe closeout and optional routes to compare notes or ask the next crew how they prefer to receive handoffs.

### Field 04 expansion — middle branch and supported consequences

The player chooses a new inspection. The current duty/task owner either accepts it or refuses because the required crew is unavailable. In the accepted branch, the inspection returns that the latch was tested and its result is recorded. The player then decides whether to reopen the station through the correct owner command. In the refusal branch, the station remains unavailable and the player can close the scenario with a clear explanation. The refusal is not treated as a lost scenario or a hidden penalty.

A disagreement branch occurs if the outgoing worker believes the test already happened but has no receipt. The player can retain both statements and ask the incoming crew to perform a new check. The later dialogue can say that the new record provides a safer reference without accusing the first worker of lying.

### Field 05 expansion — optional objective and relationship callback

One optional objective asks the player to compare the outgoing and incoming notes. Another asks them to return a borrowed tool if the inventory owner confirms custody. A third asks the incoming crew to choose a concise handoff format if current task/journal systems can store it. Skipping these objectives does not prevent the primary ending.

If a new handoff record exists, a later crew member can refer to it. If no record exists, the callback says that the station remains unavailable pending an inspection. The game does not assign a permanent “good manager” status. A player who chooses to keep the station closed can still complete the profile responsibly.

### Field 06 expansion — cross-system trace

The review traces the browser selection to campaign owner; campaign initialization to duty/site owner; inspection request to its actual handler; result to history; optional item return to inventory; and profile/run identity to the save section. Each handoff has one source path. If the objective graph needs to infer an owner result by reading private data, the design is rejected or redirected through the current public API.

Compare this run against all integrated and partial plan documents that touch duty handoffs, station interaction, journal records, and scenario launching. The collision review cites exact files and current outcomes. If an existing integration already provides a shift handoff, this scenario reuses it. If no owner exists, the profile waits rather than creating a local stand-in.

### Field 07 expansion — save and browser behavior

Save at four points: after initialization; after opening the handoff note; after requesting an inspection; and after receiving a result but before the final station command. On reload, the campaign identity, objective state, owner receipts, and available action must remain truthful. An in-flight command is reconciled with its owner; it is never blindly resent.

If the player exits to the menu, the browser labels the run as active and shows its last objective. Resuming returns to the current task. Starting another profile uses established save-slot rules. The library does not maintain a separate run list unless an existing campaign owner supports that contract.

### Field 08 expansion — accessible and fair decision review

Before the station reopen command, the UI states whether the owner’s result supports reopening and what the command changes. If no result exists, the command is unavailable with a reason. Keyboard and controller users can reach the source note, inspect result, and select a valid branch. The selected profile card and launch settings retain focus after cancellation or validation failure.

A cold reader should understand that inspection and reopening are separate actions. If they believe reading the note itself opened the station, revise the interaction language. The scenario gives no real-time penalty unless its profile explicitly names an owner-supported deadline.

### Field 09 expansion — replay and diagnostic comparison

A seeded replay should produce the same initial profile facts and objective ordering for the same inputs. If the player makes different choices, the divergence begins at the choice event and flows through owner receipts. Diagnostic output captures profile revision and rejected dependency without exporting telemetry. Compare a fresh run and a resumed run for duplicate item return, objective completion, and notifications.

Browser load, preflight, initialization, first scene, and resume are measured separately. If later content increases library size, validation should reuse catalog results only under current loader guarantees. Do not trade away deterministic ordering to improve startup.

### Field 10 expansion — worked-run acceptance outcome

The profile is ready only if the run offers a truthful refusal path, a completed inspection path, and a primary ending in which the station remains unavailable. Save/resume preserves each result. The browser promise matches the first command, and the ending names the station state and remaining responsibility. All branches use current owner calls; the authored scenario cannot grant station access by itself.

The acceptance packet records owner approvals, collision analysis, catalogs, version and slot behavior, UI flow, return behavior, and measured launch performance. If a required seam is still unresolved, keep the profile in the draft library with its exact blocker and use another owner-ready profile for the first playable anthology release.


## Pass 15 — Library seasons, profile progression, and campaign anthology content volume

This pass describes how the library can grow through releases without duplicating campaign identity, difficulty, or save ownership. All profiles remain draft until their premise and owner contracts are validated.

### Field 01 expansion — anthology seasons rather than an endless list

A library can group profiles into small editorial seasons. A season may connect profiles through a shared location, recurring character, or public record, but each profile must still function as an understandable standalone run. A season landing page explains order recommendations and callbacks without requiring completion of every profile. The player can choose any unlocked start.

Candidate first anthology: verification, communication, access, power, staffing, and stock profiles already drafted. Candidate second anthology: shift handoff, item provenance, archive relocation, delayed signal, public scheduling, and shared custody. A later anthology might examine emergency repair coordination, apprenticeship, conflicting maps, seasonal access, shelter logistics, and memory archives, provided current plan and system reviews find distinct playable gaps. These are content directions, not newly approved waves.

### Field 02 expansion — profile lifecycle states and update policy

The library tracks content status separately from campaign progress. Draft means no playable promise. Premise checked means current plans and source reviewed. Content valid means references pass. Owner ready means required runtime actions exist. Playable means end-to-end acceptance passed. Retired means new starts are disabled while active saves follow current migration policy.

A profile update changes only the profile revision. It does not silently alter difficulty or campaign rules. A bug fix to prose can be applied through localization/content versioning without changing objective state. A graph change requires the current save owner to choose whether the old graph remains, migrates, or blocks new progression.

### Field 03 expansion — content rows for later releases

| Release group | Candidate content | Player value | Promotion condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recordkeeping | Dated notes, handoffs, superseded notices | Clearer provenance decisions | Existing history owner can retain sources |
| Shared spaces | Scheduling conflict, accessibility request, maintenance closure | Visible civic tradeoffs | Site and event owners expose true state |
| Repair practice | Bounded scope, inspection, return visit | Better feedback about work | Existing maintenance owner can confirm result |
| Remote contact | Queued signal, delayed reply, stale request | Communication timing matters | Radio owner exposes delivery state |
| Shared inventory | Loan, return, unknown custody | Practical item stewardship | Canonical inventory owns transfers |
| Field access | Route uncertainty, inaccessible site, alternate meeting | Honest expedition consequences | Current travel and site owners support queries |
| Training | New volunteer, revised procedure, handoff | Survivor development through play | Existing skill/duty owner accepts actions |
| Archive | Old record, current correction, public/private audience | Campaign memory and evidence | Existing journal/archive path supports history |
| Recovery | Follow-up inspection, unresolved condition | Longer campaign consequence | Current site/incident owner emits event |
| Service planning | Demand, schedule, declined request | Player-facing coordination | Existing service/request owner has contract |

A release group may be reduced if owners are unavailable; content count is not an acceptance metric.

### Field 04 expansion — anthology throughline examples

A recurring records keeper appears in the first anthology as the author of a route note, later as a reviewer of a public notice, and finally as a mentor to a new volunteer. The callback is based on a specific source receipt and may be omitted if the earlier run was never played.

A repair apprentice moves from copying a part label to asking for provenance, then to writing a bounded maintenance handoff. The arc recognizes changed practice without granting a global skill level unless an existing progression owner supports one.

A message runner appears in the late-signal scenario and later asks whether a delayed note still matters. The player’s answer controls only that conversation unless the communication owner accepts a new message command. This allows a narrative season to feel connected without creating cross-campaign mutable flags.

### Field 05 expansion — scenario side content by player intention

Players may want to investigate, prepare, negotiate, document, or return. For each intention, create optional tasks that have a distinct result:

- Investigate: compare two sources or ask a current owner for an updated query.
- Prepare: obtain an accepted quote or identify a missing precondition.
- Negotiate: record agreement, dissent, or refusal through an existing owner.
- Document: publish or preserve a source with the correct audience.
- Return: revisit after a new owner event and compare the result.
- Repair: request a bounded action and inspect its receipt.
- Delegate: assign through duty or work owner and confirm acceptance.
- Withdraw: close a request by its source and suppress repeats where supported.
- Wait: identify what event could make the task actionable and let the player continue elsewhere.
- Conclude: archive the actual result without turning uncertainty into certainty.

This intention map helps diversify side quests while keeping them connected to playable systems.

### Field 06 expansion — portfolio unblocking report format

A scenario-to-plan report contains the profile ID, exact current plan reference, source evidence, whether the profile consumes an existing API, the missing contract if any, ownership status, save path, and proposed next action. If it is content-only, the plan owner can decide to include it in their package. If it demonstrates a missing consumer, the finding goes to the current foreman. If it requires a new architecture, it remains blocked.

The report explicitly excludes: relabeling an accepted plan as incomplete, inventing an unblocked status, changing the live queue, claiming a path, or editing shared ownership records. The scenario author can recommend a package but cannot grant itself implementation authority.

### Field 07 expansion — library journey after completion

When a run ends, the debrief links to the profile card, current objective history, primary result, optional outcomes, and unresolved questions. It offers restart or return to library through the existing campaign/save flow. A “continue campaign” action appears only when the current owner supports it. The card may show prior completion history if available, but never synthesizes it from local UI state.

The library can suggest a related profile based on shared owner families or narrative themes. Recommendations remain presentation and do not unlock or reorder content through a hidden score. The player can dismiss them.

### Field 08 expansion — fair content warnings and expectations

A profile summary communicates practical pressures, difficult subjects, and irreversible setup decisions in direct language. Warnings are factual and concise. They do not spoil every branch or use vague alarm. The scenario detail page states whether a profile requires an active campaign, uses a one-run setup, or can be replayed. These claims must match current save support.

The first objective does not conceal that its action can end a service or close access. If an owner’s consequences are not predictable at preview time, say so plainly and explain the source of uncertainty.

### Field 09 expansion — anthology-level save and performance gates

An anthology release should not add a new save schema per profile. Profile identity and revision use the current campaign owner. Objective and event state use their respective current owners. A release compatibility review compares active runs before and after the content pack update. The library validates metadata once where safe and loads selected story text on demand.

Measure startup and browser cost at release sizes of 6, 12, and 24 profiles. Separate catalog validation from scene rendering. Measure save impact by owner section, not by serialized word count. These figures guide optimization only after a real build exists.

### Field 10 expansion — production roadmap and truthful totals

The roadmap lists content drafted, premise checked, validated, owner-ready, playable, and retired separately. The playable profile total excludes disabled candidates and prose-only drafts. A package’s closing handoff reports accepted profiles and accepted objective rows, not all rows written during the planning pass.

The first public release can be intentionally small. One scenario that launches, saves, resumes, ends, and reports its result truthfully is a stronger foundation than a dozen profiles whose conditions exist only in narrative notes. Later profile waves can grow the anthology after current owners and plan collisions are reviewed.


## Pass 16 — Scenario acceptance examples and anthology status rules

This closing tranche gives the library a consistent way to distinguish completed writing from a playable start.

### Fields 01–03 — browser state examples

| Profile condition | Browser presentation | Launch behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Premise draft only | Hidden from ready list or labeled future content | No launch |
| Required catalog reference missing | Unavailable with a concise reason | Validation rejects before mutation |
| Optional side task missing | Profile remains available if primary path is valid | Optional task omitted |
| Owner preflight refuses | Required dependency unavailable | Return to browser with no partial state |
| Current run exists | Resume card with profile and latest objective | Use current save owner |
| Profile revision changed | Active run keeps or migrates by explicit policy | No silent graph replacement |
| Scenario complete | Completed card and actual result | Replay only through current slot rules |

These states prevent a content author from treating every written profile as selectable.

### Fields 04–07 — branch and library samples

The Shift Left Open profile ends with the station reopened after a supported inspection, left unavailable after a refusal, or unresolved when the owner cannot confirm. The Measure Twice profile ends with verified provenance, a held part, or a missing source. Each result has a distinct summary and a valid optional-content skip path.

The library links completed profiles by theme only when it can offer the next profile without implying a shared campaign save. A related-profile card is a recommendation, not a progression gate. The player may return to the library without beginning another run.

### Fields 08–10 — acceptance and reporting

A reviewer checks browser promise, opening prompt, first action, owner receipt, primary ending, optional omission, save identity, and replay behavior. They repeat launch with a missing reference and owner refusal to verify clean failure. They compare the completed run’s debrief with its saved history.

The live release report counts only profiles that pass end-to-end review as playable. It separately lists drafted scripts, validated references, owner-ready content, integration-ready packages, playable profiles, and retired starts. If the library has twelve written profiles but only one accepted end-to-end start, the report says one playable profile. This preserves a useful distinction between authoring volume and shipped game capability.


## Pass 17 — One scenario manifest, fully annotated

A candidate manifest for “A Shift Left Open” shows the minimum useful scenario package. Its ID and revision remain provisional. The browser summary promises a handoff review and a decision about whether a shared station can reopen. Its required references include the location, the prior shift note, the current task/duty owner, the opening objective, and the campaign start contract. Optional references include a returned tool and an additional journal fragment.

Preflight checks every required reference and asks the current owner whether it can accept the initial state. Failure returns to the library before activation. Successful initialization records the profile identity and owner receipts through the current campaign/save path. The first scene shows what is known and unknown. The first command reviews the handoff record. It does not open the station. A second command requests inspection. Only an owner-supported inspection can enable reopening.

The objective graph has a primary path to a truthful ending and optional branches for note comparison, tool custody, or crew preference. A refusal path leaves the station unavailable. An unresolved path retains the disagreement. Each branch has one completion receipt and a fallback when an optional owner is absent. No branch writes inventory, roster, or site state directly.

The browser, in-game panel, and debrief use the same meaning for profile status. The final summary says whether the station reopened, remains closed, or is unresolved, and cites the decision source. The profile revision survives save/load through the current campaign owner. An updated profile cannot silently replace the active graph.

Acceptance probes include invalid required reference, unavailable duty owner, failed inspection, player cancellation, save after initialization, save during a pending action, skipped optional task, and replay into a new slot. The reviewer checks that no state is left behind after failed launch, no duplicate objective is rewarded, and no disabled profile is counted as playable.

The implementation handoff names the current browser, campaign, duty/site, objective, and save owners; exact files claimed; data references; validation output; player-visible receipt; launch/resume behavior; and unresolved architecture decisions. If profile identity requires a new campaign or save authority, this manifest stays draft until a signed decision names the owner. The prose and graph are not approval to create that authority.


The anthology index should expose authoring status to internal reviewers without leaking implementation language into the player-facing browser. Production metadata can name required owner families, validators, and blocked references; player cards use plain descriptions such as “This start is being prepared” or omit unavailable drafts. Scenario ordering is editorial unless an existing progression owner makes it a gate. A profile can recommend a prior run but must say whether that run is actually required. This keeps the library from implying hidden prerequisites or changing progression through presentation alone. At release review, compare internal readiness and player-visible availability so that every displayed start has a valid launch path and every hidden dependency has an owner and a promotion condition.

For anthology review, also compare the first five minutes of each profile side by side. Record the first screen, first player verb, first owner response, first optional branch, and first save boundary. If two profiles produce the same sequence with only renamed characters, merge them or keep one as an alternate opening within a single profile. If they differ only because one starts with more resources, verify that the change is supported by the current campaign setup contract and does not become a hidden difficulty modifier. This review catches duplicate scenarios before prose and data volume make them expensive to untangle.

The acceptance report records which profile comparisons were reviewed and links to the current collision evidence. Recheck that evidence before promotion; a prior draft review is not permanent clearance.

## Pass 18 — Scenario-owner collision map and separation from test harnesses

This pass revises the scenario-library premise against current runtime and integration evidence. A test harness, a fixed playtest slice, a campaign, and a browsable scenario library are different products.

### Field 01 expansion — existing slice contract and its limit

Plan 54 has delivered SliceScenario and slice_seven_days.json. The data defines a seven-day sequence of beats, starting resources, one default seed, difficulty preset, survivor count, and expected action/outcome strings. The Core class hashes the scenario configuration, checks each day beat, emits a scorecard, and reports pass/fail. It is a deterministic playtest instrument; its current code does not establish a full production scenario browser, free-form objective graph runner, general campaign slot owner, or rollback-safe initializer.

The repository also has deterministic integration scenario tests such as the flagship economy and shelter scenarios. Those prove bounded cross-system behavior in tests. They are not player-facing missions. The expansion plan must not copy their test fixtures into a second campaign engine or imply that a test name creates a selectable game mode.

### Field 02 expansion — three legitimate scopes

1. **Authored campaign content:** add story beats, objectives, side quests, and callbacks to existing quest/campaign owners. No new scenario framework is needed.
2. **Playtest slice variants:** if the current SliceScenario contract and its owner accept another fixed seven-day validation profile, add it as test/playtest data under that same owner, with frozen hash and scorecard rules.
3. **General scenario library:** variable duration, browsable starts, campaign initialization, run identity, rollback, and replay require a separately approved architecture package if no current owner already supports them. Do not extend SliceScenario into a general campaign manager by editing only its data DTO.

Each proposal names which scope it belongs to. Combining all three into one “scenario library” hides the actual system boundary and makes the plan harder to verify.

### Field 03 expansion — scenario content classification rows

| Candidate content | Classification | Reuse/constraint |
|---|---|---|
| Seven-day survival slice | Existing playtest owner | Extend only through Plan 54 owner and its exact schema |
| Weather-and-route challenge | Current campaign content or slice variant | Plan 135/WeatherSystem owns weather effects |
| Outpost service visit | Existing expedition/colony story | Plan 160 owns colony and field clinic |
| Shelter construction choice | Existing construction/campaign path | Plan 156 owns build/renovation state |
| Historical archive investigation | Existing content using archive projection | Plan 162 owns history |
| Region survey challenge | Existing cartography/scouting content | Plan 163 owns map knowledge |
| Nuclear winter survival review | Existing world progression content | Plan 164 owns phases and season state |
| Cross-run epilogue | Existing campaign ending | Plans 140 and 145 own legacy and endings |
| Milestone-based completion | Existing achievement projection | Plan 149 owns achievement state |
| Integrated balance scenario | Test-only harness unless a runtime owner promotes it | Do not expose a test harness as a campaign |
| Variable-length branch graph | New runtime capability only if no current quest owner serves it | Requires architecture approval |
